title: Robust Auto-Bidding Strategies for Online Advertising

problem.claim: DSPs need auto-bidding strategies for bid shading but have limited winning-price information and associated uncertainty.

gap.claim: Existing strategies rely on accurately estimating the winning-price distribution, which is difficult under limited and uncertain information.

contributions.claim: The authors analyze how DSPs obtain winning-price information and abstract known and unknown uncertainty types.
The authors propose two robust bidding strategies: Robust Bidding for Censorship (RBC) and Robust Bidding for Distribution Shift (RBDS).
The strategies provide worst-case surplus guarantees under uncertain conditions.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on public datasets report that the robust bidding strategies consistently achieve superior surplus on test sets and under worst-case conditions.

narrative_sequence.summary: Existing bid-shading strategies predict the winning-price distribution and calculate an optimal bid.
Limited winning-price information and uncertainty make distribution estimation difficult for DSPs.
The authors analyze the information-acquisition process and identify known and unknown uncertainty.
The authors introduce RBC and RBDS with worst-case surplus guarantees.
Public-dataset experiments report superior surplus on test sets and in worst-case conditions.

source_observation.claim: When distributional information is limited and uncertain, the authors model distinct uncertainty types and design robust bidding strategies around them.

interpretation.claim: Separating known from unknown uncertainty can support decision methods with explicit worst-case guarantees.

application.claim: Use uncertainty-aware and worst-case-oriented strategies when reliable outcome distributions cannot be estimated.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that these strategies outperform alternatives beyond the reported public-dataset and worst-case experiments.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the public datasets, baselines, metrics, or experimental settings.
The abstract does not detail the mathematical formulation or proof of the surplus guarantees.
The abstract does not quantify the reported surplus improvements.
